title: Google reports a Gemma 4 response from a TPU in orbit
dek: Project Suncatcher returned a short model response from its prototype satellite, while thermal and radiation tests remain on the research schedule.

sources.title: We've received our first response from the Project Suncatcher prototype satellite, October 30
Our Project Suncatcher prototype satellite is in orbit, October 1
Behind Project Suncatcher, our moonshot to put AI in space, September 24, 2026

lede: Google reported on October 30 that its Project Suncatcher satellite had generated a Gemma 4 response in orbit earlier that week. The experiment tests whether data-center AI hardware can execute a workload after launch and return the result to Earth.

body.text: A ground station sent the prompt, and the satellite returned its answer while passing Svalbard, Norway. Google plans thermal-stress and radiation testing next. The response connects an onboard model to the ground communication path; the next engineering work concerns keeping that hardware useful under sustained operation.

Google's earlier project explanation points to near-continuous sunlight as an energy attraction. Cooling still needs heat pipes and radiators because a vacuum has no airflow to carry heat away. A larger system would also need high-bandwidth links between moving spacecraft. For infrastructure buyers, these are the measurements to follow before putting orbital capacity into a deployment plan.

buildersNote: Keep this in the research watchlist. Ask for sustained throughput, power consumption, radiation failures and launch-inclusive cost before comparing orbital compute with a terrestrial serving budget.

claims.text: Google says the prototype produced the first AI response from a data-center-class TPU in orbit.
The update establishes neither commercial availability nor sustained uptime, fleet networking or cost per useful workload.
